title: Execute Recovery, Business Continuity (BC), and Post-Incident Reviews
intro: Restoring trust and learning from incidents: recovering AI systems through trusted model rollback, clean checkpoint restoration and vector-store recovery; designing AI circuit breakers and kill switches that work under pressure; planning business continuity and disaster recovery around mapped AI dependencies; running post-incident reviews that update TTP registers and defences; and decommissioning AI systems securely, including machine unlearning and model termination.
objectives: Recover AI systems to a verified trusted state using rollback, clean checkpoints, vector-store recovery and configuration restores
Design AI circuit breakers and kill switches that act outside the model, fail safe and are tested regularly
Map critical AI dependencies and build BC/DR plans with recovery objectives, alternatives and degraded modes
Run blameless post-incident reviews and turn lessons into tracked actions and TTP register updates
Decommission AI systems securely, and choose between machine unlearning, retraining and model termination

blocks.title: Getting back to a trusted state

scenes.title: Getting back to a trusted state
scenes.sub: Rollback, clean checkpoints and vector-store recovery
scenes.say: Recovery isn’t just switching the system back on. It means returning to a state you can trust, and proving it, without losing more data or service than you have to. | This video covers recovery strategies for AI systems: trusted model rollback, clean checkpoint restoration and vector-store recovery.

scenes.title: What can be recovered, and how

items.d: Roll back to a signed registry version
Restore, then retrain on clean data
Prompts and guardrails from version control
Reset, or restore a clean copy

scenes.say: Six kinds of AI asset need recovery plans. | Models: roll back to a signed version in the registry. | Checkpoints: restore a verified clean checkpoint, then retrain or fine-tune on clean data. | Vector stores: restore an index snapshot, or rebuild the index from verified sources. | Configurations: restore prompts, guardrails and tool definitions from version control. | Agent memory: reset it, or restore a copy taken before the incident. | And datasets: return to earlier dataset versions, identified by their hashes.

scenes.title: Roll back, restore or rebuild?
scenes.say: There are three broad ways to recover. | Roll back to the previous signed version. Restore a clean snapshot or checkpoint. Or rebuild from verified sources. | Rolling back takes minutes, restoring takes hours, and rebuilding can take days or weeks. | Roll back when the previous version is known to be clean. Restore when a clean copy predates the problem. And rebuild when no trusted copy exists at all.

scenes.title: Recovering a poisoned vector store
scenes.say: Here is how to recover a poisoned vector store. Pick the most recent snapshot taken before the poisoned content arrived, using ingestion logs to be sure. | Restore it to a staging environment, not straight to production. | Re-add the legitimate changes made since the snapshot, from verified sources only. | Re-embed content if needed, making sure the same embedding model is used throughout, or vectors won’t be comparable. | Validate retrieval with golden queries that have known correct results, and with canary documents. | Then cut over, and watch retrieval and outputs closely for the following weeks.

scenes.title: Recovery objectives in practice
scenes.say: Here is how recovery objectives play out. | At two on Monday morning, a routine index snapshot is taken. It becomes the recovery point. | On Tuesday morning, poisoned documents are uploaded. | On Wednesday afternoon, the poisoning is detected and the affected retrieval is quarantined. | An hour later, service is restored from Monday’s snapshot, well within the recovery time objective of four hours. | By evening, legitimate changes made since Monday have been re-added from verified sources, so nothing of value is lost.

items: Plan recovery for models, checkpoints, indexes, configs, memory, datasets
Roll back, restore or rebuild, depending on what is trusted
Restore to staging, re-add verified changes, validate, then cut over
Set and test recovery time and recovery point objectives
scenes.say: To recap. | Plan recovery for models, checkpoints, vector stores, configurations, agent memory and datasets. | Roll back, restore or rebuild, depending on which copies you can trust. | Restore to staging, re-add verified changes, validate, and only then cut over. | And set, and test, recovery time and recovery point objectives for each AI component.

blocks.md:
### Recovery strategies
| Strategy | How it works | Requirements |
|---|---|---|
| **Trusted model rollback** | Redeploy a previous signed, approved version from the registry | Signed versions, retained artefacts, deployment pipeline that can deploy older versions (Module 3.5) |
| **Clean checkpoint restoration** | Restore a checkpoint that lineage proves predates the problem, then retrain or fine-tune on clean data | Checkpoint retention, lineage, verified clean datasets (Module 5.6) |
| **Vector-store recovery** | Restore an index snapshot, or rebuild from verified source documents | Regular, immutable snapshots; ingestion logs; recorded embedding model versions |
| **Configuration restore** | Redeploy prompts, guardrails, tools and parameters from version control | Configuration as code (Module 5.1) |
| **Agent memory recovery** | Reset memory, or restore a clean copy; remove planted entries | Memory snapshots and per-entry provenance |
| **Fallback operation** | Run a simpler model, rule-based flow or manual process during recovery | Tested fallbacks (Module 3.6) |

### Recovery objectives for AI
- **Recovery time objective (RTO):** how quickly each AI capability must be back. A fraud model may need minutes; an internal drafting assistant may tolerate days.
- **Recovery point objective (RPO):** how much recent data or change you can afford to lose: for example, the index updates since the last clean snapshot, or conversation history.
- Set objectives per component, because they differ: the model, its index, its prompts and its memory may all have different RTOs and RPOs.
- **Snapshots and backups** must be **immutable** and **retained long enough** to predate slow-burning incidents such as poisoning, which may go unnoticed for weeks.

### Recovering safely
1. **Confirm eradication first** (Module 5.6), or the attacker may still have access.
2. **Choose the recovery point** using lineage and ingestion logs, not assumptions.
3. **Restore to staging** and run safety regression tests before production.
4. **Re-apply legitimate changes** from verified sources, including approved fixes made during the incident.
5. **Cut over gradually** (canary), with tightened monitoring, and keep the fallback ready.
6. **Communicate** with users about restored service and any data lost.

For hosted models, recovery may mean switching to a different model version or provider. Test behaviour, safety and prompts on the alternative before you need it (Section 3).

blocks.title: Which recovery strategy fits?
pairs: Yesterday’s prompt change caused harmful outputs; the previous prompt was fine
Configuration restore from version control
Poisoned documents entered the index on Tuesday; Monday’s snapshot is clean
Vector-store snapshot restore, then re-add verified changes
All three recent model versions were trained on poisoned data
Clean checkpoint restoration and retraining
The current model is tampered; last week’s signed version is verified clean
Trusted model rollback
Planted instructions sit in an agent’s long-term memory
Memory reset or clean restore

blocks.title: Recovery questions
blocks.md: The best answers recover to a **verified trusted state** (signed versions, clean checkpoints, snapshots that **predate** the incident), **restore to staging and test** before production, and **re-apply legitimate changes** from verified sources. Backups that are too short-lived to predate slow poisoning, or restoring straight into production, are common traps.

q.q: A knowledge base was poisoned eight weeks ago, but the organisation keeps only 30 days of index snapshots. What does this reveal?
o: Snapshots are unnecessary, because indexes can always be repaired in place
Snapshot retention is too short to recover from slow-burning poisoning
The organisation should take snapshots every hour instead of every day
Knowledge bases should never be used for customer-facing assistants
q.why: Poisoning can go unnoticed for weeks, so retention must reach back far enough to provide a clean recovery point; otherwise the index must be rebuilt from verified sources. More frequent snapshots don’t help if none predate the poison.

sections.title: AI circuit breakers and kill switches

blocks.title: Automatic brakes and the big red button

scenes.title: Automatic brakes and the big red button
scenes.sub: AI circuit breakers and kill switches
scenes.say: Some AI failures move faster than any person can react. Others need a deliberate decision to stop everything. Circuit breakers handle the first; kill switches handle the second. | This video covers AI circuit breakers and kill switches, and how to design them so they work when needed.

scenes.title: Circuit breaker or kill switch?
rows: A whole AI system or capability
scenes.say: Circuit breakers and kill switches do different jobs. | A circuit breaker trips automatically when a threshold is crossed. A kill switch is pulled by a deliberate human decision. | A circuit breaker usually affects one path, feature or agent. A kill switch can stop a whole AI system or capability. | The system itself operates the circuit breaker. Named people with authority operate the kill switch. | And a circuit breaker resets after health checks pass, while restarting after a kill switch needs approval.

scenes.title: What an AI circuit breaker can watch

items.d: Safety classifier hits above a limit

scenes.say: AI circuit breakers can watch more than errors. | Harmful output rates: trip when safety classifiers flag too many outputs. | Agent action rates: trip when tool calls rise far above baseline. | Spend and tokens: trip when budget burn per hour exceeds a limit. | Data leaving: trip on unusual outbound volume or new destinations. | Control failures: if a guardrail or data loss prevention service is unavailable, fail closed rather than run unprotected. | And the classic reliability triggers: error rates and latency.

scenes.title: Circuit breaker states

stages.label: Half-open
stages.d: A little trial traffic after a cool-down.

scenes.say: A circuit breaker moves through states. | Closed is normal: traffic flows, and thresholds are watched. | When a threshold is crossed, the breaker trips. | Open: traffic is diverted to a fallback, such as a simpler model or a human queue, and an alert is raised. | After a cool-down, the breaker goes half-open, letting a little trial traffic through. | If the trial is healthy, it closes again. If not, it opens again, and people investigate.

scenes.title: Designing a kill switch that works

items.d: Who may pull it, at any hour
What happens to work in flight

scenes.say: A kill switch only helps if it works under pressure. Six design points matter. | It works outside the model, at the gateway, a feature flag or the identity layer, so it doesn’t depend on the model cooperating. | It is fast, taking effect in seconds across every region and instance. | Authority is clear: named people, with deputies, may pull it at any hour. | The safe state is defined: what happens to queued and in-flight work. | A fallback is ready, and people know the manual process. | And it is tested regularly, in exercises, not just written down.

items: Circuit breakers trip automatically; kill switches are deliberate
Watch harm, actions, spend, egress and control failures
Closed, trip, open, half-open: trip fast, recover carefully
Kill switches: outside the model, fast, authorised, safe, tested
scenes.say: To recap. | Circuit breakers trip automatically on thresholds; kill switches are pulled deliberately by people with authority. | AI circuit breakers can watch harmful outputs, agent actions, spend, outbound data and control failures, as well as errors. | They move between closed, tripped, open and half-open states: trip fast, recover carefully. | And kill switches must work outside the model, act fast, have clear authority, define a safe state and be tested regularly.

blocks.md:
### AI circuit breakers
Module 3.6 introduced circuit breakers as a reliability pattern for failing dependencies. For AI security and safety, the same pattern can trip on **behavioural** signals:
| Trigger | Example threshold | Breaker action |
|---|---|---|
| Harmful output rate | Safety classifier flags above 1% of outputs in 5 minutes | Route to a safer fallback model or a human queue |
| Agent action rate | Tool calls above 5× the agent’s baseline | Pause the agent; hold pending actions |
| Spend or tokens | Hourly budget exceeded | Throttle or suspend the key or application |
| Data egress | Outbound volume or destinations outside policy | Block outbound actions; alert the SOC |
| Control failure | Guardrail or DLP service unavailable | **Fail closed**: stop serving unprotected responses |

Thresholds come from baselines (Module 5.2) and the release thresholds agreed before launch (Module 5.1). Every trip should alert someone, and recurring trips are findings for the post-incident review.

### Kill switches
- **Independent of the model:** implemented at the gateway, feature flags, network or identity provider (revoking the system’s credentials), never by instructing the model.
- **Scoped options:** one agent, one capability (such as web browsing or payments), one application, or all AI use.
- **Authority and access:** named roles with deputies, available at any hour; pre-approved for defined conditions (Module 5.1).
- **Safe state:** define what happens to queued actions, in-flight sessions and users; switch to a known fallback.
- **Testing:** exercise kill switches in game days (Module 4.4), measure time to full effect, and fix what fails.
- **Records:** log who pulled it, when and why, and require approval to restore service after safety checks (Module 5.6).

The EU AI Act expects high-risk systems to let human overseers interrupt operation through a "stop" button or similar procedure that brings the system to a halt in a safe state (Article 14). Major AI developers’ frontier safety frameworks apply the same principle at the model level: they commit to pausing deployment or further development if a model reaches defined risk thresholds before adequate safeguards are in place.

blocks.title: Circuit breaker or kill switch?
pairs: Harmful outputs exceed 1% for five minutes, so traffic moves to a fallback
Circuit breaker
The CISO halts all agent payment capabilities after a confirmed compromise
Kill switch
The DLP service goes down, so responses stop until it returns
Circuit breaker (fail closed)
A regulator orders the company to stop using a scoring model
Kill switch, then decommissioning
An agent’s tool calls exceed five times its baseline and it is paused
Circuit breaker

blocks.title: Brake questions
blocks.md: **Circuit breakers** are automatic and threshold-based; **kill switches** are deliberate and authorised. Both must work **outside the model**, define a **safe state** and a **fallback**, and be **tested**. A kill switch that depends on the model obeying an instruction, or that nobody has tried, is a classic weak answer. When a protective control fails, **fail closed**.

q.q: An organisation’s "kill switch" for its customer agent is an instruction in the system prompt telling the agent to stop if it receives a special phrase. What is the MAIN weakness?
o: The special phrase is too long for staff to remember during an incident
It depends on the model obeying, which a manipulated model may not do
System prompts can’t contain any instructions about stopping
The phrase might accidentally be typed by a customer one day
q.why: A kill switch must work regardless of the model’s state, at the gateway, feature flag or identity layer. A manipulated or malfunctioning model may ignore the phrase. Memorability and accidental triggering are minor by comparison.

sections.title: Business continuity, disaster recovery and AI dependency mapping

scenes.title: When the AI isn’t there
scenes.sub: BC/DR plans and critical AI dependency mapping
scenes.say: As AI moves into core processes, its failure becomes a business continuity problem. A provider outage, a GPU shortage or a kill switch can stop work that used to run without AI. | This video covers business continuity and disaster recovery planning for AI, starting with mapping critical AI dependencies.

scenes.title: AI dependencies to map

items.d: APIs and MCP servers agents use

scenes.say: Six kinds of dependency sit behind most AI services. | Model providers: the hosted models you call, and the regions they run in. | Compute: GPU capacity, and any reservations you rely on. | Data and indexes: vector stores, data pipelines and feature stores. | Tools and connectors: the APIs and MCP servers that agents use to act. | Identity and secrets: keys, tokens and the identity providers that issue them. | And safety services: guardrails, data loss prevention and monitoring. If they fail closed, as they should, the AI service stops too.

scenes.title: Mapping one AI service
scenes.say: Here is a dependency map for one service. The customer support process depends on an AI assistant. | The assistant calls a hosted model from a single provider region: a single point of failure, so it needs a tested alternative. | It retrieves answers from a vector database, protected by daily snapshots. | It updates customer records through a CRM connector on an MCP server, which needs its own recovery plan. | And it depends on the identity provider and vaulted keys. Each dependency gets an owner, a recovery objective and a fallback.

scenes.title: Continuity needs differ
scenes.say: Business impact analysis shows that continuity needs differ widely. | A fraud detection model may need to be back within minutes, while an internal drafting assistant can wait days. | Fraud scoring can’t lose transactions. The drafting assistant can lose the last day of conversation history. | Fraud detection falls back to a rules engine with manual review. Staff can simply work without the drafting assistant. | And fraud failover is tested quarterly, while the drafting assistant’s plan is reviewed once a year.

scenes.title: AI continuity strategies
scenes.say: Six strategies keep AI services running. | A second provider or model, tested in advance for behaviour and safety, because prompts and outputs rarely transfer unchanged. | Multi-region deployment, so one region’s failure doesn’t stop the service. | A degraded mode, using a simpler model or rules, that keeps the essentials running. | Offline, immutable copies of weights, indexes and configurations. | Capacity plans for compute, reserved or with agreed burst options. | And contracts and exit plans: service levels, notice of changes and the ability to move your data and fine-tunes elsewhere.

items: Map providers, compute, data, tools, identity and safety services
Give each dependency an owner, objective and fallback
Set RTO and RPO from business impact analysis
Test alternative models, failover and degraded modes
scenes.say: To recap. | Map every AI dependency: providers, compute, data and indexes, tools, identity and safety services. | Give each one an owner, a recovery objective and a fallback. | Set recovery time and recovery point objectives from business impact analysis. | And test alternative models, failover and degraded modes before you need them.

blocks.md:
### Frameworks
Business continuity management is set out in **ISO 22301**, ICT readiness for business continuity in **ISO/IEC 27031**, and contingency planning in **NIST SP 800-34**. Sector rules add requirements: for example, **DORA** requires EU financial entities to manage ICT third-party risk, including concentration risk and exit strategies, which applies to critical AI providers.

### Critical AI dependency mapping
For each AI service that supports a critical process, record:
| Item | Example questions |
|---|---|
| **Business process and impact** | What stops if the AI stops? What is the maximum tolerable downtime? |
| **Models and providers** | Which model versions, providers and regions? Which fourth parties do they rely on? |
| **Data and indexes** | Which pipelines, vector stores and feature stores? How are they backed up, and how far back? |
| **Tools and agents** | Which APIs, MCP servers and connectors? What happens to in-flight actions? |
| **Identity and secrets** | Which keys and identities? Can they be recovered or reissued quickly? |
| **Safety and monitoring** | Which guardrails and monitoring services? Do they fail closed, and what then? |
| **People** | Who can operate, retrain or switch the system? Are skills concentrated in one person? |

### BC/DR plans for AI
- **Set objectives** (RTO, RPO and maximum tolerable downtime) per AI service from business impact analysis.
- **Plan alternatives:** secondary models or providers, multi-region deployments, degraded modes and manual processes.
- **Test alternative models properly:** switching models changes behaviour. Pre-test prompts, guardrails, safety evaluations and output formats on the alternative, and keep it ready.
- **Protect recovery assets:** immutable, off-site copies of weights, checkpoints, index snapshots, datasets and configurations, with retention long enough to predate slow-burning incidents (Section 1).
- **Watch concentration risk:** many services relying on one provider, region or model family can fail together.
- **Exercise the plans:** failover tests, game days and tabletop exercises that include AI scenarios such as provider outages, forced model retirements and kill-switch activation (Module 5.1).
- **Contracts:** availability commitments, notice of model changes and retirements, data and fine-tune portability, and support during incidents (Module 2.5).

blocks.title: The single-provider claims assistant
blocks.md: An insurer’s claims triage now runs entirely through an AI assistant that calls one hosted model in a single region. The manual triage team was disbanded last year. The provider announces that the model version will be retired in 60 days, and the same week a regional outage stops claims processing for nine hours.

q.q: Which action BEST improves the insurer’s resilience?
o: Ask the provider for compensation for the outage under the existing contract
Map dependencies, set objectives, and test an alternative model and a manual fallback
Move the assistant to a different single region with the same provider
Wait for the provider’s replacement model and switch on the retirement date
q.why: Dependency mapping, recovery objectives and tested alternatives address both outages and forced retirements, and restoring a manual fallback covers total AI loss. Compensation, another single region or a last-minute switch leave the single points of failure in place.

blocks.title: Continuity questions
blocks.md: Look for **dependency mapping** (including providers, compute, data, tools, identity and safety services), **RTO and RPO set from business impact analysis**, **tested alternatives** (models, regions, degraded and manual modes) and attention to **concentration risk**. "The provider has a 99.9% SLA" is not a continuity plan.

q.q: An organisation plans to fail over to a second model provider if its main provider has an outage. What MUST be done for this to work?
o: Nothing, because all large language models behave in much the same way
Test prompts, guardrails, safety and output formats on the second model in advance
Sign the contract with the second provider only once an outage actually happens
Ask staff to rewrite all of the prompts manually on the day of the outage
q.why: Models differ in behaviour, safety and formats, so the alternative must be prepared and tested before it is needed. Assuming equivalence, last-minute contracts and rewriting prompts during an outage all fail when it matters.

sections.title: Post-incident reviews, lessons learned and TTP registers

scenes.title: Learning from every incident
scenes.sub: Post-incident reviews, lessons learned and TTP registers
scenes.say: An incident that doesn’t change anything will happen again. The post-incident review turns a painful experience into stronger defences. | This video covers post-incident reviews, turning lessons into actions, and updating the register of attacker tactics, techniques and procedures.

scenes.title: A post-incident review
scenes.say: A post-incident review follows six steps. Schedule it promptly, within days of the incident closing, while memories are fresh. | Gather the record: the timeline, evidence, decisions log and root cause analysis. | Hold a blameless review with every role that took part, from the SOC to legal and communications. | Agree the findings: what worked, what didn’t, and why. | Turn them into actions, each with an owner, a due date and a way to verify it. | And share the lessons, then track every action to closure.

scenes.title: Questions a good AI review asks

items.d: And how could it be detected sooner?

scenes.say: A good AI post-incident review asks six questions. | How was the incident detected, and how could it have been detected sooner? | How quickly was it contained, and what slowed containment down? | Did the playbooks fit, and did they cover this AI scenario? | Did escalation work: were roles, authority and timing clear? | Were legal duties met, including notification clocks and contractual commitments? | And what would have prevented it: which controls, design changes or processes?

scenes.title: Updating the TTP register
scenes.code:

notes.d: The TTP register records how attackers have operated against you.
A name, its ATLAS mapping and when it was first seen.
Which systems are exposed to this technique.
The detections and mitigations now in place.
Regression tests that run on every release.
Intelligence passed to peers, with sharing limits.

scenes.say: A TTP register records how attackers have actually operated against you, and what you have done about it. | Each entry names the technique, maps it to MITRE ATLAS and records when it was first seen. | It records which systems are exposed: here, research agents that can fetch web pages. | It lists the detections and mitigations now in place. | It points to regression tests, such as the incident replay set, that run on every release. | And it records what was shared with peers, here a sector ISAC, under traffic light protocol amber.

scenes.title: Lessons learned or lessons applied?
scenes.say: The difference between lessons learned and lessons applied is follow-through. | Filing a report isn’t enough; actions must be tracked to closure. | A playbook left unchanged repeats the same mistakes; update it, and exercise the change. | Noting a detection gap doesn’t close it; deploy and test a new rule. | And intelligence kept internal helps nobody else; share it with ISACs and partners.

items: Review promptly, blamelessly, with every role
Ask about detection, containment, playbooks, escalation, duties, prevention
Turn findings into owned, dated, verified actions
Update the TTP register, threat models and detections; share
scenes.say: To recap. | Review every significant incident promptly and blamelessly, with every role involved. | Ask about detection, containment, playbooks, escalation, legal duties and prevention. | Turn findings into actions with owners, dates and verification, and track them to closure. | And update the TTP register, threat models, detections and tests, and share what you learned.

blocks.md:
### Post-incident reviews
NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3 (2025) aligns incident response with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 and treats lessons learned as part of **continuous improvement** across all functions, not a single final step. In practice:
- **Timing:** hold the review within days to two weeks of closure; for long incidents, hold interim reviews.
- **Participants:** the incident lead, SecOps, MLOps, data science, model and data owners, legal, privacy, communications and any key suppliers.
- **Blameless:** focus on systems, controls and decisions under real conditions; people speak openly only if they aren’t punished for honest mistakes (Module 5.6).
- **Metrics:** time to detect, time to contain, time to recover, notification timeliness, and impact (data, users, cost).
- **Outputs:** a short report, a prioritised action list with owners and dates, and updates to playbooks, runbooks, threat models, risk registers, training and exercises.

### What to update after an AI incident
| Artefact | Typical updates |
|---|---|
| **TTP register** | New or changed techniques, mapped to ATLAS and ATT&CK, linked to detections, mitigations and tests |
| **Threat models** | New attack paths and assumptions that failed (Module 6.1) |
| **Detections** | New rules and baselines; tuning to reduce noise (Modules 5.2 and 5.3) |
| **Regression suites** | Incident replay sets added permanently (Module 5.6) |
| **Playbooks and runbooks** | Steps that were missing, slow or unclear (Module 5.1) |
| **Risk and vulnerability registers** | Updated likelihood and impact; new findings (Module 5.4) |
| **Training and exercises** | Scenarios based on what actually happened |
| **Supplier management** | Contract, assessment and monitoring changes for providers involved (Module 6.3) |

### The TTP register
A **TTP register** is an internal catalogue of adversary tactics, techniques and procedures observed against the organisation or its sector. Each entry records the technique, its ATLAS or ATT&CK mapping, exposed systems, detections, mitigations, regression tests and sharing status. It connects incidents to defences and keeps knowledge from leaving with individual staff.

### Sharing lessons
Share indicators and techniques through ISACs, partners and, where appropriate, AI providers, using **STIX and TAXII** and the **Traffic Light Protocol (TLP)** to signal how widely information may be passed on (Module 5.2). Remove personal and sensitive data first, and follow legal advice.

blocks.title: Post-incident terms
cards: A structured, blameless review of an incident that produces owned, dated and verified improvement actions.
An internal catalogue of attacker techniques seen against you, linked to detections, mitigations and tests.
Labels such as TLP:CLEAR, GREEN, AMBER and RED that tell recipients how widely they may share information.
The time from detection to stopping an incident from causing further harm; a key response metric.
Findings that have led to verified changes, not just a report.

blocks.title: Post-incident questions
blocks.md: The best answers hold a **prompt, blameless** review, produce **owned, dated, verified actions**, and update **playbooks, detections, regression tests, threat models and the TTP register**. Sharing with **ISACs** using **TLP** is good practice. A report that sits on a shelf, or a review that looks for someone to blame, is the classic wrong answer.

q.q: Six months after an AI incident, the same type of attack succeeds again. The post-incident report had recommended a new detection rule. What is the MOST likely failure?
o: The original post-incident review was held too soon after the incident
The action had no owner, date or verification, so it was never applied
The attackers were noticeably more skilled and better prepared the second time
The report was too long for busy managers to read through in full
q.why: Lessons only help when actions are owned, scheduled, verified and tracked to closure. Without that, recommendations stay on paper and the same gap is exploited again.

scenes.title: Retiring AI safely
scenes.sub: Decommissioning, disposal, unlearning and model termination
scenes.say: Every AI system eventually ends: replaced, failed, unlawful or simply no longer needed. A model that is switched off but not properly retired leaves keys, data and copies behind. | This video covers secure decommissioning and disposal, and remediation through machine unlearning and model termination.

scenes.title: What decommissioning must cover

items.d: APIs, apps, agents that call it

scenes.say: Decommissioning has six parts. | Endpoints and integrations: the APIs, applications and agents that call the model. | Credentials and identities: API keys, agent identities and tool grants that must be revoked. | Model artefacts: weights, checkpoints and fine-tuned versions, including copies held by providers. | Data: training sets, embeddings, vector stores, logs and caches. | Records: the registry, inventory, AI bill of materials and model card, updated to show the system is retired. | And dependants: the users and downstream systems that relied on it, who need notice and an alternative.

scenes.title: A decommissioning sequence
scenes.say: A secure decommissioning follows six steps. The model owner approves retirement, and users and dependent teams are given notice. | Traffic stops: endpoints are disabled and callers switch to the replacement. | Access is revoked: API keys, agent identities, tool grants and service accounts. | Artefacts and data are archived or destroyed, according to retention rules and any legal holds. | Storage is sanitised and the result verified, including deletion confirmations from providers that hold fine-tunes or uploaded data. | And records are updated: the registry marks the model as retired, the inventory and AI bill of materials change, and a certificate of sanitisation is filed.

scenes.title: Unlearn, retrain or terminate?
scenes.say: When data must be removed from a model, there are three options. | Machine unlearning tries to remove specific data’s influence. Retraining rebuilds the model without the data. Termination retires the model entirely. | Unlearning is hard to verify. Retraining gives strong assurance. Termination is complete. | Unlearning can suit narrow removal requests, where its effect can be checked. Retraining suits poisoned or unlawfully obtained data. And termination suits risks that can’t be fixed, or cases where a regulator or court orders it.

scenes.title: Copies that are easy to forget
scenes.say: Six kinds of copy are easy to forget. | Copies held by providers: fine-tuned models, uploaded training files and logs. | Backups and disaster recovery replicas, off-site and in other regions. | Developer environments: laptops, notebooks and test storage buckets. | Replicas of vector stores, and cached answers. | Derived models, such as distilled or fine-tuned versions. | And evaluation sets and logs, whose recorded outputs may contain the very data you are removing.

items: Decommission endpoints, access, artefacts, data, records, dependants
Notify, stop, revoke, archive or destroy, sanitise, record
Unlearn narrowly; retrain for poison; terminate when unfixable
Hunt down copies: providers, backups, laptops, replicas, derivatives
scenes.say: To recap. | Decommissioning covers endpoints, access, model artefacts, data, records and dependants. | Notify, stop traffic, revoke access, archive or destroy, sanitise and verify, then update the records. | Use unlearning narrowly, retrain to remove poisoned or unlawful data, and terminate models whose risks can’t be fixed. | And hunt down every copy: at providers, in backups, on laptops, in replicas and in derived models.

blocks.md:
### When to decommission
Triggers include end of life or replacement, unfixable vulnerabilities (Module 5.4), failed revalidation, loss of the legal basis for the training data, a regulator’s or court’s order, contract termination with a provider, and business decisions. ISO/IEC 5338 (AI system life cycle processes) and ISO/IEC 42001 treat **retirement** as a planned life-cycle stage, not an afterthought.

### Secure disposal
- **Sanitise media** in line with NIST SP 800-88 Revision 2 (2025): match the method to data sensitivity and media type, then **verify and document** the result (Module 3.4).
- **Crypto-shredding:** where data is encrypted with dedicated keys, destroying the keys makes the data unreadable, which helps with distributed copies and backups.
- **Provider deletion:** request and record deletion of fine-tuned models, uploaded files and retained logs, according to the contract; obtain written confirmation (Module 2.5).
- **Retention and legal holds:** some records must be kept, such as logs required by law or evidence under a legal hold. Archive them securely, and destroy everything else on schedule.
- **Certificates:** file a certificate of sanitisation or destruction, and update the registry, inventory and AIBOM.

### Remediation: unlearning and termination
- **Machine unlearning** aims to remove the influence of specific training data without full retraining. Exact methods (such as training in shards so only affected parts are retrained) give stronger guarantees; approximate methods are cheaper but **hard to verify**. Use unlearning for narrow requests where its effect can be tested, and record the method and evidence.
- **Retraining without the data** is the strongest way to remove poisoned or unlawfully obtained data short of termination.
- **Model termination** retires the model, its derived models and its data. Regulators have ordered it: the US Federal Trade Commission has required companies to delete models and algorithms built with improperly obtained data, a remedy known as **algorithmic disgorgement**, in cases such as Everalbum (2021), WW International’s Kurbo app (2022) and Rite Aid (2023).
- **Personal data in models:** the European Data Protection Board’s Opinion 28/2024 says AI models trained on personal data can’t always be considered anonymous, which affects how erasure requests and unlawful processing must be handled (Module 3.2).

### Decommissioning checklist
1. Owner approval and notice to users and dependent teams.
2. Endpoints disabled; callers moved to the replacement or fallback.
3. All credentials, identities and tool grants revoked.
4. Artefacts and data archived or destroyed per retention and legal holds, including provider copies, backups, replicas, developer copies and derived models.
5. Sanitisation verified and documented.
6. Registry, inventory, AIBOM and model card updated; monitoring and detections for the retired system removed or repurposed.

blocks.title: Which remediation fits?
pairs: A user asks for their data to be removed, and the model barely relied on it
Machine unlearning, with verification, or retraining
Training data turns out to have been collected unlawfully
Retraining without the data, or termination
A regulator orders deletion of models built with improperly obtained images
Model termination (algorithmic disgorgement)
A model is replaced by a new version at the end of its life
Planned decommissioning and secure disposal
A vendor still holds a fine-tuned copy after the contract ends
Provider deletion with written confirmation

blocks.title: Decommissioning questions
blocks.md: Strong answers decommission **completely**: revoke credentials, remove **every copy** (providers, backups, replicas, laptops, derived models), respect **retention and legal holds**, **verify** sanitisation, and update **records**. For removing data from models, remember that **unlearning is hard to verify**; retraining or termination gives stronger assurance. "We switched off the endpoint" is not decommissioning.

q.q: A company retires a customer-facing model by disabling its endpoint. Months later, an audit finds the model’s API key still works through another route, and a fine-tuned copy remains at the provider. What was missing?
o: A press release announcing the model’s retirement to all of its customers
Full decommissioning: revoke access, remove copies, verify, update records
A longer notice period before the endpoint was finally switched off for good
An evaluation of the model’s accuracy carried out just before it was retired
q.why: Disabling one endpoint leaves credentials and copies behind. A complete process revokes access, removes or archives every copy, including provider-held ones, verifies the result and updates the records.

quiz.q: Why should a vector store be restored to staging before production?
o: Staging restores are cheaper because they use less powerful hardware
So retrieval can be validated and verified changes re-added safely
Production systems can’t accept restored data under most licences
Restoring to staging deletes the poisoned documents automatically
quiz.why: Staging lets the team re-add legitimate changes and test retrieval with golden queries and canaries before users depend on it.

quiz.q: What does a recovery point objective (RPO) describe?
o: How quickly a service must be restored after any disruption
The amount of recent data or change you can afford to lose
The point in a process where AI first becomes involved
The location of the backup data centre used for recovery
quiz.why: RPO sets how far back recovery may go; RTO sets how quickly service must return.

quiz.q: Why must snapshot retention reach back far enough for AI recovery?
o: Older snapshots are always smaller and faster to restore than new ones
Poisoning can go unnoticed for weeks, so a clean point must predate it
Regulators require every snapshot to be kept for at least ten years
Newer snapshots can’t be restored once an incident has been declared
quiz.why: If every retained snapshot already contains the poison, the only option is a slow rebuild from verified sources.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a circuit breaker and a kill switch?
o: Circuit breakers are hardware; kill switches are always software
Breakers trip automatically; kill switches are pulled deliberately
Kill switches only affect test environments, never production
There is no difference; the terms are used interchangeably
quiz.why: Circuit breakers respond to thresholds without waiting for people; kill switches are authorised human decisions to stop a capability.

quiz.q: Why must a kill switch work outside the model?
o: Models are usually far too slow to process stop instructions in an emergency
A manipulated or failing model may not obey an instruction to stop
Kill switches inside models are prohibited by the EU AI Act
External kill switches are cheaper to build than internal ones
quiz.why: Gateways, feature flags and credential revocation work regardless of what the model does.

quiz.q: What should an AI service do if its guardrail service becomes unavailable?
o: Continue serving responses, because availability matters most
Fail closed: stop or divert traffic until the protection returns
Switch to a larger model, which is less likely to be manipulated
Ask users to report any harmful responses they receive meanwhile
quiz.why: Running without a protective control exposes users and data; failing closed, with a fallback, is the safe default.

quiz.q: Why must a second model provider be tested before it is needed?
o: Contracts with second providers can only be signed after testing
Models differ in behaviour, safety and formats, so prompts may not transfer
Second providers always charge more for models that are untested
Testing in advance guarantees both providers will never fail together
quiz.why: Switching models changes behaviour, so prompts, guardrails, safety evaluations and output formats must be prepared in advance.

quiz.q: What is concentration risk in AI continuity planning?
o: The risk that staff lose concentration during long incident calls
Many services depending on one provider, region or model family
The risk that GPUs overheat when too many models run at once
A measure of how much data is concentrated in a single index
quiz.why: When many services share one dependency, a single failure can stop them all at once.

o: Nobody is allowed to mention any mistakes that were made
It focuses on systems, not blame, so people share what happened
The review is written by an external firm with no internal input
Only senior managers attend, so junior staff aren’t blamed
quiz.why: People speak openly about decisions and mistakes only when the aim is to fix systems, not punish individuals.

quiz.q: What does a TTP register link together?
o: Staff training records and their certification expiry dates
Observed attacker techniques and the defences and tests for them
Third-party contracts with AI suppliers and their termination clauses
Tokens, transactions and payments processed by AI agents
quiz.why: The register connects what attackers have done with the detections, mitigations and regression tests that now address it.

quiz.q: What does TLP:AMBER signal when sharing threat intelligence?
o: The information may be published openly, on any public website or forum
Share only on a need-to-know basis within your organisation and clients
The information is unverified and should not be acted upon at all
The incident is still active and the sender needs urgent help
quiz.why: TLP labels set sharing limits: AMBER allows limited disclosure on a need-to-know basis within the recipient organisation and its clients.

quiz.q: Why is disabling a model’s endpoint not enough to decommission it?
o: Endpoints can’t be disabled without the model provider’s permission
Keys, identities, artefacts and data copies remain until removed
Disabled endpoints restart automatically after thirty days
Decommissioning is only complete once the model is retrained
quiz.why: Leftover credentials and copies keep risk alive; decommissioning removes or archives them and verifies the result.

o: A technique for compressing models so they use less memory
An order to delete models built with improperly obtained data
A method for extracting training data from a model’s outputs
A process for splitting a model across several providers
quiz.why: The US FTC has used this remedy to require deletion of models and algorithms derived from unlawfully obtained data.

exam.q: A support assistant’s model was tampered with. Last week’s signed version is verified clean, and the prompts and index haven’t changed since. What is the FASTEST trustworthy recovery?
o: Rebuild the model from scratch using freshly collected training data
Roll back to last week’s signed version from the registry, then monitor
Restore the whole platform from the oldest backup that is available
Keep the tampered model running while a new one is being trained
exam.why: A verified clean, signed version can be redeployed in minutes. Rebuilding is slow, the oldest backup loses legitimate changes, and the tampered model must not keep serving.

exam.q: A poisoned vector store is restored from a clean snapshot taken five days ago. Legitimate policy updates were added during those five days. What should happen to them?
o: Discard them, because anything added after the snapshot may be poisoned
Re-add them from verified sources, then validate retrieval before cutover
Copy them across directly from the poisoned index to save time
Ask employees to remember the policy changes and re-enter them
exam.why: Verified sources restore legitimate content without bringing the poison back, and validation confirms retrieval works. Copying from the poisoned index risks reintroducing it.

exam.q: An agent’s tool calls suddenly rise to ten times its baseline in two minutes, at 03:00 when nobody is watching. Which control would have limited the impact MOST?
o: A weekly report of agent activity sent to the agent’s business owner
A circuit breaker that pauses the agent when action rates exceed a threshold
A kill switch that only the CEO is authorised to activate, in person, on site
A policy forbidding agents from running outside business hours
exam.why: An automatic breaker acts in seconds without waiting for people. Reports are too slow, a CEO-only kill switch is impractical at night, and policies don’t stop running agents.

exam.q: During a game day, the team finds that pulling the kill switch for a customer agent takes 40 minutes to take effect across all regions. What should happen?
o: Accept it, because kill switches are rarely needed in practice
Treat it as a finding: redesign for speed, retest, and track the fix
Remove the kill switch entirely, since it clearly doesn’t work as intended
Ask staff to pull the kill switch 40 minutes earlier in future
exam.why: Exercises exist to find exactly this. A slow kill switch must be fixed and retested; accepting, removing or working around it leaves the gap.

exam.q: A bank’s fraud model depends on a single GPU cluster in one region, and its manual review team has been reduced. Business impact analysis sets an RTO of 15 minutes. What is the BEST continuity improvement?
o: Increase the RTO to 24 hours, so that it matches current capability
A tested secondary deployment and a rules-based degraded mode
Buy more GPUs for the same cluster in the same region
Ask the fraud team to work overtime whenever the model is unavailable
exam.why: A tested secondary deployment meets the RTO, and a degraded mode keeps essential screening running. Changing the RTO ignores the business need; more GPUs in one region keep the single point of failure.

exam.q: Which item is MOST important to include in an AI dependency map for a critical service?
o: The service’s user interface design and accessibility features
Providers, regions, data stores, tools, identity and safety services
The names of all the staff who have used the service in the past year
The marketing plan and budget for promoting the service to customers
exam.why: Continuity depends on the technical and supplier dependencies that can fail, each with an owner, objective and fallback.

exam.q: An AI incident’s post-incident review produced 14 recommendations. Six months later, three have been implemented and nobody knows the status of the rest. What is the BEST fix?
o: Hold another review to produce a fresh set of recommendations
Give each action an owner, date and verification, tracked to closure
Reduce the number of recommendations in future reviews to three
Close all the remaining recommendations, since the incident is now quite old
exam.why: Lessons become improvements only when actions are owned, scheduled, verified and tracked. More reviews, fewer recommendations or closing them unaddressed don’t fix the process.

exam.q: After an indirect injection incident, which update BEST captures the knowledge for future defence?
o: A note in the incident ticket describing the attack in general terms
A TTP register entry linked to ATLAS, detections, mitigations and tests
An email to all staff warning them about suspicious web pages
A reminder in the system prompt telling the agent to ignore injections
exam.why: A structured register entry connects the technique to concrete defences and regression tests. Ticket notes get lost, staff emails don’t protect agents, and prompt reminders are weak controls.

exam.q: A fine-tuned model must be removed because its training data was collected unlawfully. Which remediation gives the STRONGEST assurance?
o: Apply an approximate unlearning method, and assume that it has worked
Terminate the model and its derived models, deleting the unlawful data
Add a guardrail that blocks outputs mentioning the unlawful data
Restrict the model to internal users, so that fewer people ever see its outputs
exam.why: Termination, including derived models and the data, removes the unlawful processing completely. Approximate unlearning is hard to verify, and guardrails or restrictions leave the model in use.

exam.q: A company ends its contract with an AI provider that hosted its fine-tuned model and stored training files. What should the decommissioning process include?
o: Nothing, because the provider’s data is the provider’s responsibility
Deletion of the fine-tune, files and logs, with written confirmation
Asking the provider to keep the files in case they are needed again
Downloading the files to a personal laptop for safekeeping
exam.why: Provider-held copies are part of the decommissioning scope; deletion should be requested and confirmed in writing, in line with the contract.
